Short version, as of September 2026:

- You do not need an OpenAI API key to use Entire runners.
- You do not need GitHub Actions or another GitHub CI system first.
- You can define multiple review runners.
- “Ready to merge” with a one-approval Entire gate and zero approvals is not explained by GitHub lacking an approval requirement; that looks like bypass, stale configuration, or a UI/gate bug.
- Building → Reviewing is a handoff/readiness transition, not something runner completion causes.

## Entire runners versus GitHub CI

They are parallel systems triggered by similar events:

```text
git push
├── Entire
│   ├── run risk/confidence/security/review runners
│   ├── attach findings and monitor values to the Trail
│   └── evaluate Entire gates
│
└── GitHub
    ├── run .github/workflows/*.yml, if any
    ├── publish test/build/deployment checks
    └── enforce GitHub branch protection
```

| | Entire runner | GitHub Actions runner |
|---|---|---|
| Configuration | `.entire/runners/*.json` | `.github/workflows/*.yml` |
| Runs where | Isolated cloud sandbox managed through Entire | GitHub-hosted or self-hosted Actions machine |
| Purpose | AI review, risk, drift, confidence, security | Build, unit tests, lint, deploy, arbitrary automation |
| Requires the other? | No | No |

Entire can ingest GitHub check results into its `checks` gate, but that is optional. If you have no GitHub workflows, Entire’s API explicitly models the checks status as `none`; the AI runners can still run normally. Entire can also post its aggregate gate as a GitHub check, but that does not turn the Entire runner into a GitHub Actions job. See the [Entire runner definition](https://docs.entire.io/glossary#runner) and [published API contract](https://entire.io/api/openapi.json).

## Do you need an OpenAI API key?

No, not for the default runner path.

The runner set in this repository uses `runtime.kind: "prompt_runner"` and `runtime.agent: "claude"`; the review runner selects Sonnet specifically: [trail-review.json](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/main/.entire/runners/trail-review.json:1). Your monitor and review already completing successfully is practical confirmation that runner execution is provisioned.

There is a separate operation that sounds similar:

```bash
entire runner setup --yes --agent codex
```

Here, Codex is used locally to tailor the JSON configuration. It is not the eventual Trail runner. Codex itself supports either ChatGPT subscription login or API-key login, so even that operation does not inherently require an API key. [Official OpenAI authentication documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth) confirms both methods.

So:

- Entire cloud runner execution: no OpenAI key required.
- Local Codex used for configuration tailoring: use your existing Codex login; API-key auth is optional.
- Direct OpenAI API calls from your own program: those do require an API key.

## Multiple review runners

Yes—the current data model supports multiple runners.

Each should have:

- A unique filename and `id`.
- Its own prompt and preferably a distinct focus.
- `"trails_review": {"enabled": true}`.
- `"output": {"adapter": "last_json_line", "result_type": "code_review_comments"}`.
- A push trigger if it should run automatically.

For example:

```text
.entire/runners/
├── trail-correctness.json
├── trail-performance.json
├── trail-simplification.json
└── trail-security-review.json
```

The API exposes results by `runnerId`, returns a list of runners on a Trail, allows a gate to reference multiple `runner_ids`, and returns the number of review runners launched on a rerun. That structure is explicitly plural rather than singleton. [Published OpenAPI](https://entire.io/api/openapi.json).

One caveat: runners launched simultaneously may see the same initial `previous_findings` snapshot, so two broad prompts can independently report the same bug. Keep their mandates orthogonal:

- Correctness: concrete behavioral regressions.
- Performance: measured or structurally unavoidable cost.
- Simplification: unnecessary complexity, without duplicating correctness.
- Security: trust boundaries, credential exposure, authorization.

All findings should attach as they arrive. The findings gate can then block on the combined set of unresolved findings.

## Why “Ready to merge” with zero approvals?

It should not be because GitHub has no minimum-approval rule.

There are two independent policies:

1. GitHub branch protection: determines whether GitHub permits its PR to merge.
2. Entire’s approval gate: determines whether Entire considers its Trail gates satisfied.

The published API has a first-class `approvals` gate definition with its own `blocking`, `enabled`, and `config` fields. Entire can enforce that independently of GitHub branch protection. It can optionally publish the combined result back to GitHub as a check run.

If the Entire gate says minimum approvals `1`, zero approvals should not produce an unqualified Entire “Ready to merge” state. I would check:
